{{Short description|American mathematician and civil engineer (1858–1923)}}
'''Charles Newton Little''' (1858–1923) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[civil engineering|civil engineer]]. He was known for his expertise in [[knot theory]], including the construction of a [[Knot tabulation|table of knots]] with ten or fewer crossings.<ref name="sud">{{citation|url=http://stanforddailyarchive.com/cgi-bin/stanford?a=d&d=stanford18931122-01.2.2&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-------|title=C. N. Little: Professor of Pure Mathematics|newspaper=[[The Stanford Daily]]|date=November 22, 1893}}.</ref><ref name="science">{{citation
 | last = Lehmer | first = D. N. | authorlink = Derrick Norman Lehmer
 | date = October 1923
 | doi = 10.1126/science.58.1503.299
 | issue = 1503
 | journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]]
 | pages = 299
 | title = Charles Newton Little
 | volume = 58| pmid = 17735747 | bibcode = 1923Sci....58..299L }}.</ref>

Little's father was a missionary to [[Madurai]], in India, where Little was born in 1858;<ref>Birthdate from the ''Stanford Daily''; Lehmer's obituary in ''Science'' states the birthdate as 1865.</ref> his family returned with him to America in 1859.<ref name="sud"/> He earned an A.B. from the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln|University of Nebraska]] in 1879, and continued at Nebraska's Institute of Mathematics and Civil Engineering, where he earned an M.A. in 1884.<ref name="sud"/><ref name="science"/> After this, he entered graduate study at [[Yale University]], and completed his Ph.D. in 1885 under the supervision of [[Hubert Anson Newton]], with a dissertation concerning knot theory.<ref name="sud"/><ref name="science"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=22376}}</ref>

He returned to the University of Nebraska as an associate professor of civil engineering, and was promoted to full professor in 1889. In 1893 he joined [[Stanford University]] as a professor of pure mathematics, after turning down a chair of mathematics at Nebraska.<ref name="sud"/>
In 1899–1900 he went on leave from Stanford, and traveled to Germany to study mathematics with [[Felix Klein]] and [[David Hilbert]].<ref name="science"/><ref name="idaho">{{citation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uLBGAQAAMAAJ&pg=RA1-PA17|title=University of Idaho General Catalog, vol. XIV, no. 5|date=June 1919|page=17}}.</ref>
He moved again in 1901 to the [[University of Idaho]], as a professor of civil engineering, and in 1911 was appointed as dean of engineering there.<ref name="science"/><ref name="idaho"/>

He died on September 7, 1923, of heart failure, in [[Berkeley, California]].<ref name="science"/>
